A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CoreCognition and Concept Hacking. Their main text, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies create specific uncertainties but do not prevent comparison of the work.

before.justification: v3 reports original MLLM evaluations, human responses, correlation and scaling analyses, prompting experiments and Concept Hacking results.

after.justification: v4 reports original benchmark and Concept Hacking results, supplemented by reasoning-model comparisons, statistical tests and subgroup analyses.

M1.justification: Appendix D revises answer matching: v3 names Llama3.1-70B and DeepSeek, whereas v4 specifies a four-LLM fallback requiring agreement from at least three judges. The central 12-concept framework and label-inverting Concept Hacking procedure remain.

E1.justification: The 12 cognitive domains, 45 Concept Hacking pairs and external benchmark coverage remain. However, v3 explicitly includes multiple-video questions, while v4 lists only single-image, single-video and multiple-frame inputs. The PDFs do not establish whether those scenarios were removed or converted to frames, so coverage changes cannot reliably be separated from formatting and sample-selection changes.

E2.justification: Table 2 substantially changes its reported comparison set, expanding from 16 models to 30 and adding a reasoning-model category, including GPT-o1, QVQ-72B-Preview and Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking. Section 4.5 adds explicit comparisons between reasoning models and instruction-tuned counterparts. Older selected entries such as NVLM-D-72B disappear from Table 2, without establishing their exclusion from the entire study.

E3.justification: Circular scoring changes from requiring every option rotation to be correct to averaging correctness across rotations. The reported benchmark size changes from 2,519 questions in v3's main text, or 2,299 in its appendix, to 1,503 in v4. Quality-control criteria and subgroup evaluation designs also change. v4 reports 230 retained models, although Appendix D still states 219.

E4.justification: v4 adds reasoning-versus-instruction comparisons, raw-versus-normalized accuracy checks, and extensive robustness analyses across input capabilities, model competence and prompts in Appendices G–I. It also quantifies matching-method comparisons. The prompting study and GPT-4o Concept Hacking case study already existed in v3 and are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: v4 adds paired t-tests for developmental-stage contrasts, p-values for reasoning-model comparisons and explicit 95% confidence-interval labels on scaling plots. v3 contains descriptive distributions and unlabeled uncertainty bands but no corresponding formal tests. These additions do not establish additional repeated runs or seeds.

E6.justification: Table 2 broadly replaces model and human scores and adds many results. For example, GPT-4o spatiality changes from 38.82% to 67.95% under revised data and scoring conditions. Correlation values, scaling estimates and prompting distributions also change. New reasoning, matching and subgroup results substantially extend the empirical record.

T1.justification: v4 removes v3 Appendix D.2's erroneous equation defining failure rate as the fraction successfully matched to valid choices. No new theorem or proof is introduced; the added normalization and t-test formulas mainly explain statistical procedures.

C1.justification: The core-deficit hypothesis and benchmark contributions remain. The abstract and introduction qualify v3's categorical absence-of-scaling claim as reduced or absent scalability relative to higher-level abilities. Claims about illusory understanding are reframed around core deficits and shortcut reliance.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive limitations concerning linguistic and perceptual confounds, exclusion of nonlinguistic models and Concept Hacking's scalability. It broadens incorrect-control outcomes from illusory understanding to core deficits, expands interpretations of prompting and reasoning results, and proposes explicitly teaching core knowledge before large-scale pretraining. Appendix H newly identifies unreliable permanence assessment in the small single-image subset.

D1.justification: Reproducibility documentation is substantially reworked. v4 adds annotator qualifications, validation rounds, 43 isolated inference environments, scheduling and sanity checks, and exact ensemble judges. It removes v3 Appendix C's detailed per-domain construction, toolkit and source descriptions. The stated A100 hardware remains unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work expands to include multimodal model development and shortcut-learning research. v4 explicitly positions CoreCognition relative to M3GIA, MARVEL and DevBench, and adds substantial literature on reasoning, scaling and model limitations. These are substantive positioning changes beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: Large portions of the introduction, related work, curation, experimental discussion and conclusion are rewritten. The prompting study moves from Appendix F into Section 4.6, cognitive-framework subsections are consolidated, and the appendices are extensively reorganized. Terminology and author/publication information also change.

P2.justification: v4 adds a curation diagram, reasoning comparisons, statistical tables and multiple robustness panels. Table 2 gains a mean column and reasoning category. Existing examples, heatmaps and Concept Hacking graphics are redrawn or rearranged; normalized accuracy loses its logarithmic display. Several formerly large figures become compact single-column displays.

improvement.justification: Compared with v3, v4 strengthens the evidence through raw-versus-normalized and subgroup robustness checks, reasoning-model comparisons and explicit measurement limitations. These gains are tempered by unreconciled 230-versus-219 model counts, differing stage-test statistics in Figure 4 and Table 6, and removal of useful curation details. The evidence supports a limited net improvement.
